set.approach: Start at the Grotto Falls trailhead and follow the Hyalite Creek trail up the canyon, passing the Amphitheater area and then the Arch Falls sign (stay left there). After a small creek crossing the trail reaches an open meadow; just beyond it a climbers' trail cuts left and switchbacks up through the trees, and the Dribbles flows come into view above and to the left. Check the avalanche forecast before committing to the gully below the flows.
set.descent_text: Parties usually rappel. One option uses the trees well to climbers' right of the route: from the farthest-right clump (usually equalised with cord) rappel past the thin runnel to a bolted anchor, then rappel again to the ground. Check that nobody is climbing the runnel before throwing ropes. Another option uses the trees far to climbers' left to reach a bolted anchor on a rock slab, then the ground. A third is to walk left from the top to the neighbouring Avalanche Gulch and rappel from a tree and a large dead tree there.

review.notes: Approach from the route page and the Dribbles area page (they agree on the trail, Arch Falls sign, meadow and left-cutting climbers' trail). Descent options from the route page only; rope counts and times left out.

set.approach: Reach the base of the Dribbles by the Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead (past the Amphitheater area and the Arch Falls sign, then the meadow and the climbers' trail left through the trees). From the foot of the Dribbles, traverse right through the trees under the cliff. Once the woods give way to a steep snowfield, Silken Falls is the evident waterfall there.
set.descent_text: Parties rappel the route. After the first pitch you can rappel from a V-thread, or continue to the bolted anchor at the top of the second pitch and rappel from there.

review.notes: Route page: traverse right from Dribbles base to the snowfield; V-thread/bolted anchor on pitch 2; protection line says screws and v-threads. Trail to Dribbles base from area page.

set.approach: Follow the Dribbles approach: the Grotto Falls trailhead, the Hyalite Creek trail past the Amphitheater area and Arch Falls sign, the meadow, then the climbers' trail left through the trees. At the foot of the Dribbles, go left for a short distance to the next drainage and follow that gully up. The snow sections of the gully can slide, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route from V-threads.

review.notes: Route page: go climbers' left at base of Dribbles to next drainage; descend by rapping the route on V-threads; warns snow pitches can slide.

set.approach: Approach as for Avalanche Gulch: the Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead to the Dribbles, then left to the neighbouring drainage. Climb the first moderate ice step, continue up the snow gully, and just before the steep canyon holding the harder upper pitches of Avalanche Gulch take the obvious bench that heads left. Follow the bench at about the same height until Responsible Family Men is in view, in the first flow left of Avalanche Gulch. For the easier start, backtrack right to a short low-fifth-class band, climb it to a narrow bench, and follow the exposed fourth-class ledge to a small alcove at the base of the ice. The more difficult starts descend into the gully instead. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Approach from the route page (detailed); the Avalanche Gulch page gives the first leg. No descent stated.

set.approach: Take the Dribbles approach: the Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead past the Amphitheater area and Arch Falls sign, the meadow, then the climbers' trail left through the trees to the base of the Dribbles. The Dribbler is a thin variation beside the Dribbles, just to its right, and it shows clearly from the base in years when it forms.

review.notes: Location is 'just right of Dribbles' on route page; trail from Dribbles pages. No descent stated.

set.approach: Approach as for Avalanche Gulch: the Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead to the Dribbles base, then left to the neighbouring drainage and up the gully. The line is a variation on the crux pitch of upper Avalanche Gulch, starting behind and beneath the alcove under the dagger. The gully holds avalanche-prone snow, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Descend as for Avalanche Gulch, by rappelling the route from V-threads.

review.notes: Route page says approach and descent are as for Avalanche Gulch; the Avalanche Gulch page gives rap the route on V-threads.

set.approach: The climb sits directly above Silken Falls. It is usually reached from lower Avalanche Gulch or the Dribbles: take the Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead to the Dribbles area, then work up the drainages to the top of Silken Falls. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page: directly above Silken Falls, approached from lower Avalanche Gulch/Dribbles. Fallen page confirms the Silken Gully continues above Silken Falls. No descent stated.

set.approach: Take the Dribbles approach (Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead, past the Amphitheater area and Arch Falls sign, then the climbers' trail left). Climb Silken Falls and keep going up the gully until the route is visible on your right. You can also cross into the Silken gully from above the Dribbles or from lower Avalanche Gulch. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page location for the gully; trail from area page. No descent stated.

set.approach: Walk the Dribbles approach up the Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead, but at the second small clearing in the woods peel off right onto a seldom-used climbers' trail. It leads up to the east face of Palace Butte; when you reach the wall, go left. The route is on the northeast face at the foot of a major avalanche gully, left of Kansas Cornfield, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route.

review.notes: Route page for approach, avalanche exposure and rappel descent; Kansas Cornfield page agrees on the turn-off and the wall. Rap count left out (one source).

set.approach: Follow the Dribbles approach up the Hyalite Creek trail from the Grotto Falls trailhead, then at the second small clearing in the woods peel off right onto a seldom-used climbers' trail. It climbs to the east face of Palace Butte; at the wall, go right. The flow sits at the bottom of a significant avalanche gully, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Climb until the ice eases into snow, then build an anchor there and rappel. A further small ice step lies higher if you want to continue.

review.notes: Approach agrees between this page and Hang Time's. Descent from this route's own page.

set.approach: The route sits on the big north face of Palace Butte, overlooking Hyalite. Climb Twin Falls to reach the large cirque above, then hike south (left) toward the face with a distinct snow and turf band partway up. The line begins at the right-hand end of the face, climbing Palace Butte Falls first. The face can also be reached by the gentler back side of the butte.
set.descent_text: Parties either walk off the back side of the butte or rappel the route. If rappelling, mind where the ropes run on the first traversing rappel.

review.notes: Route page: Twin Falls to the cirque, hike south, start at Palace Butte Falls; walk-off or rappel. Area page: north face reached by climbing Twin Falls or the mellower back side. Rappel count left out (one source).

set.approach: In winter the road to the Granite Lake trailhead near Libby is unplowed past the end of the pavement, so the trip starts on skis or foot or by snowmobile and is long; the summer trail then follows Granite Creek to the lake, best kept on the north side for the first part before crossing. Baby Lincoln Falls is a short ice step right beside the approach trail to Granite Lake, next to a good camp spot on Granite Creek. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route and sub-area pages: on the Granite Lake approach, near a creekside camp spot. Granite Lake area page: winter road/trail along Granite Creek. No descent stated.

set.approach: From the north end of Granite Lake, ski left beneath and then above the Three Tiers cliffs, swing back right, and follow the drainage uphill toward A Peak. After a short while you reach a large clearing with the wall on its far side. The wall faces east, so it catches more sun than much of the area, and the approach crosses slide-prone ground, so check the avalanche forecast. The line is the main ice gully in the middle of the wall.

review.notes: Wall approach from the wall's area page; position from route page. No descent stated (tree anchor at the top only).

set.approach: From the north end of Granite Lake, ski left beneath and then above the Three Tiers cliffs, swing back right, and follow the drainage uphill toward A Peak. After a short while you reach a large clearing with the wall on its far side. The wall faces east, so it catches more sun than much of the area, and the approach crosses slide-prone ground, so check the avalanche forecast. The line is the main flow on the wall, with a gully to its left and a large hanging dagger to its right.

review.notes: Approach from the wall's area page; position from route page. No descent stated.

set.approach: From the north end of Granite Lake, ski left beneath and then above the Three Tiers cliffs, swing back right, and follow the drainage uphill toward A Peak. After a short while you reach a large clearing with the wall on its far side. The wall faces east, so it catches more sun than much of the area, and the approach crosses slide-prone ground, so check the avalanche forecast. Green Oasis is the farthest line up the wall, starting with a short easy corner before the thin ice on the face.

review.notes: Approach from the wall's area page; position from route page. No descent stated.

set.approach: From the north end of Granite Lake, ski left beneath and then above the Three Tiers cliffs, swing back right, and follow the drainage uphill toward A Peak. After a short while you reach a large clearing with the wall on its far side. The wall faces east, so it catches more sun than much of the area, and the approach crosses slide-prone ground, so check the avalanche forecast. The line follows moderate ice up to a shark-tooth shaped rock feature.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the tree at the rock feature.

review.notes: Approach from the wall's area page; the route page says rappel from a tree at the rock feature.

set.approach: Walk down the Bear Creek trail and continue a short way past the sign marking the Wilderness boundary. Leave the trail heading north, cross the creek, and climb the hillside to the cliff line, then walk left (west) along its base. The flow is hard to spot until you are beneath it, after which it is obvious. It faces south at low elevation, so it relies on cold, cloudy weather.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route from trees.

review.notes: Route page for approach and tree rappels. Area page lists the two routes only.

set.approach: Two ways in. On foot, hike the Bear Creek trail beneath the Morning Thunder Wall and its big rounded granite slab, cross the creek, and go up the largest couloir; the climb is at the top. In winter, when the overlook road allows, you can park at the first right-hand switchback, ski uphill and sidehill across to the rim above the Morning Thunder Wall, and rappel in to the climb from there. The walking route is the more straightforward. The route faces south over smooth granite, so it needs cold weather.

review.notes: Both approaches from the route page. No descent stated.

set.approach: From the Beehive Basin trailhead, which is on Beehive Basin Road near the Big Sky Mountain Village, follow the well-worn trail to the lake in the basin at the foot of the cirque. The Prow is the well defined spire you pass; the peak is the one farther back. The route begins in the 4th of July Couloir and leaves it about a third of the way up, above the first black rocks, into an obvious left-leaning snow gully.
set.descent_text: Either scramble or rappel down the couloir on the west side to get back into the 4th of July Couloir. The rock there is loose, so descend carefully.

review.notes: Approach: basin and peak area pages; start from route page. Descent from route page only; distances left out.

set.approach: From the Beehive Basin trailhead, follow the well-used trail to the lake in the basin at the base of the cirque. The Prow, a well defined spire, is on the way; continue past it to the main peak behind. Five Magics is a snow and ice line on the Beehive, two lines right of the Standard Route.

review.notes: Peak area page for the trail, route page for position. No descent stated for this line (area page's general couloir descent not applied).

set.approach: The Going-to-the-Sun Road is closed to vehicles for much of the winter, so most of the season the approach starts by walking or skiing the road to the Avalanche Lake campground, then taking the Avalanche Lake trail to the lake and crossing it to the far end of the basin. Bring skins or snowshoes. Most of the climbing faces north in a shaded basin, so watch for spindrift and check the avalanche forecast. The flow sits between two larger flows, below the feature called the Monument where the lake meets the cliff face.
set.descent_text: Rappel from a tree to the right of the top; a V-thread also works.

review.notes: Area page for approach; route page for position and the tree/V-thread rappel.

set.approach: The Going-to-the-Sun Road is closed to vehicles for much of the winter, so the approach begins by walking or skiing the road to the Avalanche Lake campground, then the Avalanche Lake trail, then across the lake to the far end of the basin. Allow a multi-day trip; a backcountry permit is advised. From the base of Screws As Desired, traverse across to the bottom rock band, gaining some height. The flow is tucked in a corner next to an avalanche chute, below and to the right of the feature called Memorandum, and the traverse crosses the chute's start, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Area page and route page. Mileage left out (single source). No descent stated.

set.approach: In winter the road is closed, so the trip starts at the Lake McDonald Lodge parking lot: ski or walk up the Going-to-the-Sun Road, passing Logan Creek, then head up to the base of the falls. Expect a multi-day outing and get a backcountry permit if camping. Far Right Flow starts at the far right of the falls in a chimney-like gully with rock on its right. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Area page for approach, route page for start. No descent stated.

set.approach: The Many Glacier road is closed in winter, so reaching Grinnell Lake is a multi-day trip on skis or snowshoes (sled or bike where the road allows); the final stretch is unmarked and goes through trees, so route-finding matters. The climb is the tall waterfall on the far side of the lake, and the lake needs to be frozen enough to cross. A permit is advised for overnight trips. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Area page for approach, route page for position. No descent stated (route page only describes topping out toward the upper lake).

set.approach: The Many Glacier road is closed in winter, so the trip is a long ski or snowshoe in. The climb is near the head of Lake Josephine: just north of the Cataract Creek bridge at the end where the lake is fed, take the north shore trail and, within a short distance, head uphill into the trees to the ice. It is south facing and short.
set.descent_text: Build an anchor at the trees above the ice, then walk off down the Grinnell Glacier Trail.

review.notes: Route page for position and walk-off; area page for winter access.

set.approach: From the Lake McDonald Lodge parking lot, hike the Snyder Creek trail to the large lake. Continue around the left (north) side to bypass the cliffs, then cut back across toward the foot of the face, above Upper Snyder Lake. The route follows the obvious left-facing corner on the north face of Mt. Edwards. The face holds snow-catching basins, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Descend on V-threads.

review.notes: Area page for trail, route page for position and V-thread descent.

set.approach: Park in the village of Silver Gate and follow the plowed local street across from the outfitter south for a couple of blocks to where it bends left, then turn right onto a popular local ski trail through the forest. Keep going until the ice appears up to the left. Alternatively park near the park's northeast entrance and ski due south to the same spot. The route is inside Yellowstone, and Cooke City ice is often avalanche prone, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page for approach; area page for the general ski and avalanche note. No descent stated.

set.approach: Leave the car close to the Silvertip Mountain Center in Silver Gate, walk west along the highway a short way, and turn right to follow the ravine; or ski through the lot of the closed motel and angle northwest through the spruce glades, staying left of the burned area. Stay on the right-hand side of the drainage, since its final stretch can be avalanche prone after new snow. Skis or snowshoes are needed.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the big spruce at the top left of the route, which carries many rappel slings.

review.notes: Route page for approach and the spruce rappel anchor. Time and distance omitted.

set.approach: The flow faces south and can be seen by looking north from the highway near the park's northeast entrance station. Cooke City ice is reached on skis or snowshoes, often breaking trail, and is frequently avalanche prone, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page for position, area page for the ski access. Thin; no descent stated.

set.approach: Start from the East Rosebud trailhead parking past the campground and follow the trail along the lake, continuing beyond its end. The trail passes a stretch blasted into the rock; shortly after, the climb comes into view. Either traverse up toward it to meet the creek drainage or keep on the trail farther to meet the creek lower down, then follow the drainage up to the base, over easy ice ramps and a short initial step. It is a long, early-start day, and the headwall is exposed to avalanche, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: From the top of the headwall, rappel from a tree on climbers' right, then rappel or downclimb depending on the snowpack. Some parties finish in the gully to climbers' right of the route.

review.notes: Route page for approach and descent. Time and elevation omitted (single source).

set.approach: From Roscoe, drive west up the East Rosebud road into the canyon. Leave the car by the beaver pond shortly after the pavement begins. The ice can be seen in the unburned trees south of the road, in a narrow, north-facing canyon a short distance north of Hell Roaring Creek; the approach is brief.
set.descent_text: Walk off or rappel from trees at the top of the route.

review.notes: Route page.

set.approach: The line is on the Giants Belly wall, seen when looking south up the canyon. The approach is long. Follow East Rosebud trail 15 (the Beaten Path) for a short distance, and before Elk Lake turn left up an obvious gully that splits the walls. Top it out and go south over scree through a meadow along Fivemile Creek, then more scree and slabs to the foot of the wall. Ice Dragons follows a weakness left of the middle of the wall.
set.descent_text: The walk-off is preferred: from the plateau, cross the flat to the right and go down a northwest-trending scree slope to rejoin your upward tracks at the head of the gully, and follow the gully out. Rappelling the route is possible with double ropes and a rack but is the lesser choice.

review.notes: Route page. Distance, gain and time omitted (single source).

set.approach: From Roscoe, drive west up the East Rosebud road into the canyon. You can see the top of the route from the forest boundary sign. Keep going beyond the sign and a Forest Service information pullout (a photo on the route page shows the line that minimises bushwhacking). Then push through frozen swamp, beaver ponds and deadfall, cross the river, enter the drainage, and scramble up rocks and a short easy ice section into the base of the amphitheater. Flotation is useful in deep snow.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the tree anchor at the top, which has rings.

review.notes: Route page only.

set.approach: From the lot at the road end beside East Rosebud Lake, head south along the trail onto the first knoll by the lake end. Leave it and climb the hillside to the left; some hundreds of feet up, the falls appear up and slightly left. Finish with a boulder scramble up the slope to the base.
set.descent_text: Rappel from a tree.

review.notes: Route page only; elevation figure omitted.

set.approach: The glacier lies above the south end of Avalanche Lake, below the north face of Granite Peak. Two approaches exist. One goes via Mystic Lake and Huckleberry Creek, with bushwhacking, talus, a possible creek ford or marsh, and camping on the lake's west shore, then talus and grassy ledges up to the glacier. The other climbs the Phantom Creek trail, reached from either the East or West Rosebud trailheads, to the Froze-to-Death plateau near Tempest Mountain, or drops from the col between Tempest and Granite to a camp above Avalanche Lake.
set.descent_text: The glacier is normally climbed to reach the higher routes on the north face, and from the top parties follow the standard descent east; if camped low by Avalanche Lake, drop down from the saddle with Tempest. To retreat, rappel from V-threads or bollards until the slope is easy enough to downclimb.

review.notes: Route page only for both.

set.approach: In winter the road to the Granite Lake trailhead near Libby is unplowed past the end of the pavement, so the trip starts on skis or foot or by snowmobile and is long, then the trail follows Granite Creek to the lake. The face rises above the lake. The couloirs funnel snow, so check the avalanche forecast. Looking up from the lake, the huge central couloir of Canmore Wedding Party stands out. The next large couloir to its right splits the face diagonally up and right, and this route climbs it, then follows the corner system above.
set.descent_text: From the top, follow the ridge south, past the summit toward Snowshoe Peak, watching for large cornices on the crest. Past a small knoll, in the next saddle, drop over the east side to a steep slope leading to a flat bench, follow the bench south until a steep couloir between cliffs lets you break east, and contour down the valley and back north to Granite Lake, going around the far end of the Three Tiers cliff band.

review.notes: Route page for line and descent; area pages for trail. Elevation figures omitted.

set.approach: In winter the road to the Granite Lake trailhead near Libby is unplowed past the end of the pavement, so the trip starts on skis or foot or by snowmobile and is long, then the trail follows Granite Creek to the lake. The face rises above the lake. The couloirs funnel snow, so check the avalanche forecast. Canmore Wedding Party takes the big central couloir, which is the first feature you notice looking up at the face from the lake.

review.notes: Position from this route's page and Knickerbocker's. Descent only vaguely stated (a saddle south of the summit) so omitted.

set.approach: In winter the road to the Granite Lake trailhead near Libby is unplowed past the end of the pavement, so the trip starts on skis or foot or by snowmobile and is long, then the trail follows Granite Creek to the lake. The face rises above the lake. The couloirs funnel snow, so check the avalanche forecast. The route climbs the right-most major couloir on the face, just right of both Canmore Wedding Party and The Stumbling Stone. It is entered through a hidden approach couloir; the firmest snow is on the debris fan it deposits.

review.notes: Route page; trail from area pages. Route tops out on the summit ridge through a cornice; no descent stated.
